entities.name: 1383–1385 Portuguese Interregnum
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The 1383–1385 Portuguese Interregnum was a pivotal event in world history that took place in Portugal, shaping the Mediterranean region and setting the stage for the Age of Exploration. It began on April 10, 1383, when King Ferdinand I of Portugal died without an heir, sparking a civil war between rival claimants to the throne.

The conflict saw the rise of John I, a young nobleman who would go on to unite the warring factions and establish the House of Aviz, a dynasty that would rule Portugal for the next three centuries. The interregnum ended on October 1, 1385, when John I defeated the Castilian forces at the Battle of Aljubarrota, securing his claim to the throne.

The Portuguese Interregnum had significant consequences for the region, leading to the growth of the Portuguese navy and the establishment of trade routes with West Africa and Asia. It also laid the groundwork for the Age of Exploration, which would see European powers, including Portugal, establish colonies and trading posts around the world.

As historian Luis de Máximo noted, 'The Portuguese Interregnum was a crucible that tested the mettle of Portugal's nobility and forged the nation's identity as a maritime power.'

The event's legacy can be seen in the modern-day Portuguese nation, which continues to celebrate its rich history and cultural heritage. From the stunning architecture of Lisbon's Belem Tower to the vibrant festivals and traditions of the Algarve region, the Portuguese Interregnum's impact is still felt today.
